news_summary: A significant archaeological discovery in Denmark sheds light on early farming history through the remains of a man who witnessed its arrival.
news_summary_fr: Une découverte archéologique majeure au Danemark apporte un éclairage sur les débuts de l'histoire de l'agriculture grâce aux restes d'un homme qui a été témoin de son apparition.
news_summary_es: Un importante hallazgo arqueológico en Dinamarca arroja luz sobre los orígenes de la agricultura gracias a los restos de un hombre que fue testigo de su aparición.

articles.title: Skeleton found in Denmark came from man who witnessed the arrival of farming
articles.summary: Clues about the diet of “Rødhals Man”, who lived some 6000 years ago, hint that he lived through one of the most revolutionary changes in human history
articles.content:
Clues about the diet of “Rødhals Man”, who lived some 6000 years ago, hint that he lived through one of the most revolutionary changes in human history

The skull and arm bones of Rødhals Man John Lee, Danish National Museum & Anders Fischer, Marie Louise Jørkov, Laboratory of Biological Anthropology/Antiquity Publications Ltd

Analysis of a skeleton from Denmark, nicknamed “Rødhals Man”, hints that the individual lived through one of the most fundamental changes in human history: the transition from hunter-gathering to farming.

“What was it like to live through such a momentous transition, seeing the archipelago where your ancestors had fished being transformed by the arrival of a new group of people?” says Anders Fischer at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden.

Rødhals Man lived some 6000 years ago, and was discovered on the small island of Sejerø in Denmark in the 1950s, buried in a shell midden – an ancient accumulation of discarded sea shells and other domestic refuse. Previous investigations have indicated he was unusual. He lived some time between about 3800 and 3900 BC, near the start of the Neolithic period in the area, when diets changed to consist predominantly of terrestrial food produced by farmers. And yet Rødhals Man, with his genetic ancestry typical of the local Mesolithic Ertebølle culture of hunter-gatherers, didn’t seem to have eaten that diet: a study in 1981 indicated that he ate mainly seafood.

“There was something wrong and it is always when things don’t fit that you may be on the track of something important,” says Fischer.

To get a better idea of what was going on, Fischer and his colleagues have now looked at the levels of rare isotopes of elements including carbon, nitrogen and sulphur in several of the man’s bones, which renewed at different rates during his life, preserving different snapshots in time. The researchers also analysed the chemical signatures in one of his teeth, which preserve a record of diet from childhood. Collectively, the data gave the team an opportunity to look for clues about how Rødhals Man’s diet changed over the 30 to 40 years of his life.

“You can see that most of the time, the primary food source is what we call the eelgrass biotype. This is not eelgrass itself, but the animals that live in the thick forests of this sea grass in shallow water,” says team member John Meadows at Kiel University in Germany. This could have been animals like molluscs, flatfish or eels, he says.

But from the age of about 11 onwards, Rødhals Man’s diet became unlike that of any Mesolithic hunter-gatherer recorded so far, with increasing amounts of terrestrial, probably farmed, protein.

Rødhals Man’s burial also shares more similarities with burials of Early Neolithic farmers than those of Late Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, because his bones lacked an added coating of ochre staining and his grave featured a stone frame.

The evidence leads Meadows to suggest that Rødhals Man interacted with the Neolithic farmers and adopted some components of farmer culture while maintaining the way of life of his ancestors on the small island. Sejerø is just 12 square kilometres in area, but is only about 5 kilometres from Zealand, which is around 7000 square kilometres.

“He was on a tiny island with very little in the way of wild terrestrial resources to live on,” says Meadows. “He may have spent part of the year living in a farming community on Zealand and part living on the island and only eating fish.”

“It is quite amazing that all this information could be retrieved from one single skeleton,” says Mathias Currat at the University of Geneva. “I think this is an interesting story, which probably represents part of the main story in this area.”

It would be unusual to change diet in this way, says Marcello Mannino at Aarhus University in Denmark. “Such cultures were often very conservative in terms of their dietary habits, because diet was interlinked with the subsistence practices that shaped that culture together with religious and cosmological views of the world.”

He says it is likely that the Neolithic farmers probably first occupied areas where soil conditions were better, such as in central Zealand, and were slower to inhabit more marginal areas. “We need to find more human remains that span the transition to try to understand how it happened,” he says.

articles.personality_title: Skeleton in Denmark reveals life during farming’s arrival 6,000 years ago
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Around 6,000 years ago, people in parts of Europe were changing from hunting and gathering food to farming it. This was a huge change in how humans lived. 

**What happened** – Scientists studied the bones of a man called “Rødhals Man” found on a small Danish island. He lived during this big change and was buried in an old pile of shells. By examining chemicals in his bones and teeth, researchers learned about his diet over many years. They found he ate mostly seafood as a child but began eating more farmed foods after age 11. His grave also showed signs of mixing hunter-gatherer and farming traditions.

**Impact** – This skeleton shows how one person lived right when farming was arriving in northern Europe. It suggests that some people tried new farming foods while still keeping their old ways. This helps us understand how cultures slowly changed instead of switching all at once. It also shows how people could live between both worlds, especially on small islands near farming areas.

**What’s next step** – Experts want to find more skeletons from this time to see if others had similar diets and lifestyles. This will help explain how farming spread and how people adapted to it in different places.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The bones of Rødhals Man offer a rare glimpse into how people lived and ate during the first arrival of farming in northern Europe.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un squelette au Danemark révèle la vie lors de l’arrivée de l’agriculture il y a 6 000 ans
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Il y a environ 6 000 ans, les peuples d’Europe changeaient leur mode de vie, passant de la chasse et la cueillette à l’agriculture. Ce fut une transformation majeure pour l’humanité.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques ont étudié les os d’un homme surnommé « l’homme de Rødhals », découvert sur une petite île danoise. Il vivait au moment de ce grand changement et était enterré dans un tas ancien de coquillages. En analysant les éléments chimiques dans ses os et dents, les chercheurs ont découvert que, enfant, il mangeait surtout des fruits de mer, puis qu’il a commencé à consommer plus d’aliments issus de l’agriculture après ses 11 ans. Sa tombe montre aussi un mélange de traditions de chasseurs-cueilleurs et d’agriculteurs.

**Impact** – Ce squelette montre comment une personne vivait à l’arrivée de l’agriculture en Europe du Nord. Il suggère que certains essayaient les aliments agricoles tout en gardant leurs anciennes habitudes. Cela aide à comprendre que les changements culturels se faisaient peu à peu, et que certaines personnes vivaient entre deux mondes, surtout sur de petites îles proches des terres agricoles.

**Prochaine étape** – Les experts souhaitent trouver d’autres squelettes de cette époque pour voir si d’autres avaient des modes de vie et des régimes similaires. Cela permettra de mieux comprendre la diffusion de l’agriculture et les adaptations des populations.

**En une phrase** – Les os de l’homme de Rødhals offrent un aperçu rare de la vie et de l’alimentation lors des débuts de l’agriculture en Europe du Nord.
articles.personality_title_es: Esqueleto en Dinamarca revela vida durante la llegada de la agricultura hace 6,000 años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Hace unos 6,000 años, las personas en partes de Europa cambiaron su forma de vivir, pasando de cazar y recolectar a cultivar sus alimentos. Este fue un cambio muy grande para la humanidad.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos estudiaron los huesos de un hombre llamado “Hombre de Rødhals” encontrado en una pequeña isla danesa. Vivió durante este gran cambio y fue enterrado en un antiguo montón de conchas. Al analizar los químicos en sus huesos y dientes, los investigadores descubrieron que cuando era niño comía principalmente mariscos, pero desde los 11 años empezó a consumir más alimentos cultivados. Su tumba también muestra una mezcla de tradiciones de cazadores-recolectores y agricultores.

**Impacto** – Este esqueleto muestra cómo vivía una persona justo cuando la agricultura llegaba al norte de Europa. Sugiere que algunas personas probaron los alimentos de los agricultores mientras mantenían sus viejas costumbres. Esto ayuda a entender que los cambios culturales ocurrían poco a poco y que algunas personas vivían entre dos mundos, especialmente en islas pequeñas cerca de tierras agrícolas.

**Próximo paso** – Los expertos quieren encontrar más esqueletos de esta época para ver si otros tenían dietas y estilos de vida similares. Esto ayudará a explicar cómo se extendió la agricultura y cómo la gente se adaptó.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los huesos del Hombre de Rødhals ofrecen una visión única de cómo vivían y comían las personas al inicio de la agricultura en el norte de Europa.
